intro: You want a new book, a trip to the zoo and a pizza party. But you have only so much money and so much time. Every day, you have to choose. So does your family, your school and your town. This unit is about those choices.

First you will learn why we cannot have everything, and what we give up when we choose. Then you will visit a pizza shop and a paper airplane race. You will see how people make things, and why splitting up work helps.

By the end, you will be able to name the next-best thing you give up in a choice. You will sort resources into three groups. You will use a decision grid, and you will explain why people depend on each other.
bigQuestion: How do people make good choices when they cannot have everything they want?

Ford's company starts a moving assembly line to build cars faster

Families, schools and towns still face scarcity and make choices every day

test.why: Only the next-best choice, the library, is the opportunity cost.
A sewing machine is a tool people made to make other goods.

A store gives a free drink with every 5 visits. What is the free drink?

The barber gives a service, so the barber is a producer.

Why does the division of labor often make more goods?
choices: Each worker gets fast at one step
It needs fewer resources of every kind
test.why: Repeating one step builds skill and saves switching time.

What does a decision grid list down the side?

test.why: Stores depend on trucks, and people depend on stores.

test.why: A line goes only as fast as its slowest step, 3 a minute.

write.prompt: Your class has $100 (an example amount) and three ideas: a game day for $60, new art supplies for $90, or a class plant garden for $40. Make a decision grid. Choose one idea. Name your opportunity cost, show the money left over, and explain why your choice is best.
tips: Put the choices across the top and what matters down the side.
Show the money: $100 minus the cost of your choice.
Name your opportunity cost: just the next-best idea.
Say one good thing you give up by not picking it.

title: Scarcity and the Choices People Make

chapters.title: Why We Cannot Have Everything
chapters.bigQuestion: If we cannot have everything we want, how do we choose well?

story.title: Four Ideas and $200
story.kicker: The student council has money for one big idea, and four good ones to pick from.
paragraphs: The student council met in Room 9 after lunch. Mr. Diaz wrote a number on the board: $200. "This is our money for the spring," he said. "We get to decide how to use it." Five council members sat up straight.

Hands went up fast. Leo wanted new balls for recess, about $150 (an example price). Priya wanted a class trip to the nature center, about $200. Sam wanted a movie night with popcorn, about $120. Grace wanted new books for the library corner, about $180.

Mr. Diaz added up the ideas. Together they cost $650. "That is much more than $200," Priya said. "We cannot do all of them." Leo sighed. "Maybe we can only do one." The room got quiet while everyone thought.

Grace had a plan. "Let's make a chart," she said. "We can list what matters most. How many kids does it help? How long does it last?" They drew a grid on the board. Soon each idea had a score, and a hard choice began to look clearer.
story.think: If the council picks the books, what do they give up? Which idea would you choose, and why?

sections.title: Wants Bigger Than What There Is

lessons.title: What Scarcity Means
lessons.mainIdea: Scarcity means our wants are bigger than the things we have to meet them.
reading: The council had $200. Their four ideas cost $650 in all. They wanted more than their money could buy. This problem has a name. It is called *scarcity*.
Scarcity is not just about money. A day has only 24 hours. A park has only so much grass. A class has only one teacher. Our *wants* keep growing, but time, land and money run out.
Everyone faces scarcity, rich or poor. A rich person still has only 24 hours a day. So people must choose. Scarcity is the reason economics exists. Economics is the study of how people choose.

words.d: when people want more than there is to go around, so they must choose
things people would like to have or do

look.title: One Saturday
look.text: It is Saturday. You want to play soccer, visit your cousin, go to the library and finish a puzzle. Each takes about three hours. You are awake about 13 hours, and chores and meals take four of them.
look.prompt: How many of these things can you fit? Which one would you drop first?

check.q: What is scarcity?
choices: Wanting more than there is to go around
A store running out of one toy
check.why: Scarcity means wants are bigger than what there is. It happens even when you have some money.

check.q: The council had $200. The ideas cost $650. How much more did the ideas cost than the money?
Does a very rich person face scarcity?
choices: No, rich people can buy everything
Only if they lose their money
No, scarcity is only about money
Yes, they still have only 24 hours a day
check.why: Time is scarce for everyone. So everyone must choose.

lessons.title: Needs and Wants
lessons.mainIdea: Needs keep us alive and safe; wants make life nicer, and both must fit what we have.
reading: Food, water, a home and warm clothes are *needs*. We need them to live and stay safe. A new video game is a want. It is nice to have, but we can live without it.
Families often pay for needs first. Say a family has $100 left for the week (an example). Groceries cost $70. That leaves $30 for wants, like a movie or a toy.
Some things can be both. You need shoes. But you may want shoes with lights. The plain pair meets the need. The extra money for lights pays for a want.

words.d: things people must have to live and be safe, like food and a home
things people would like to have or do

look.title: The Shopping List
look.text: Mom's list says: milk, bread, a winter coat for Jay, a puzzle, apples and a new phone case. She has enough money for five of the six things.
look.prompt: Sort the list into needs and wants. Which thing should Mom leave off?

check.q: Which one is a need?
check.why: A warm coat keeps you safe in cold weather. The others are wants.

check.q: A family has $100 for the week (an example). Food costs $70. How much is left?
Plain shoes cost $30. Shoes with lights cost $45 (example prices). How much of the price pays for the want?
check.why: The plain pair meets the need. The extra $45 minus $30, or $15, pays for the lights.

lessons.title: Scarcity Everywhere
lessons.mainIdea: Families, schools and towns all face scarcity, so they all have to make choices.
reading: Families face scarcity. There is only so much pay each month. A family may save for a car or take a trip. It may not be able to do both this year. It has to pick.
Schools face scarcity too. A school has only so many rooms and so much money. It might add a music room or a science lab. With one empty room, it must pick one.
Towns face scarcity. A town may want a new pool and a new fire truck. Taxes pay for both, and tax money runs out. Leaders must choose what comes first.

words.d: when people want more than there is to go around, so they must choose
picking one thing from two or more options

look.title: The Empty Lot
look.text: A town owns one empty lot near the school. Some people want a playground. Some want a parking lot. Some want a garden. The lot can hold only one of them.
look.prompt: Who would be helped by each idea? Which would you pick for the lot?

check.q: A school has one empty room. It wants a music room and a lab. Why can't it have both?
check.why: There is only one room. When something is scarce, you must choose.

check.q: Which group faces scarcity?
check.why: Every group has limits on money, time or space, so every group must choose.

check.q: Where does a town get much of the money for a fire truck?
check.why: Towns pay for things like fire trucks mostly with tax money, and that money runs out.

lessons.title: Natural Resources
lessons.mainIdea: Natural resources are gifts of nature, like soil, water and trees, that we use to make things.
reading: To make anything, we need *resources*. Resources are the things used to make goods and services. Some come straight from nature. These are *natural resources*.
Illinois has rich, dark soil. Farmers use it to grow corn and soybeans. Lake Michigan gives Chicago its drinking water. Trees give wood for tables and paper.
Natural resources are scarce too. A farm has only so many acres. If a farmer plants 100 acres of corn, those acres cannot grow soybeans that year. Land has a limit.

words.d: the things used to make goods and services
things from nature used to make goods, like soil, water and trees

look.title: One Pencil
look.text: Look at a yellow pencil. The wood came from a tree. The gray middle is graphite, dug from the ground. The eraser is made from rubber or plastic.
look.prompt: Which parts of the pencil came from nature? Can you think of one more natural resource in your classroom?

check.q: Which is a natural resource?
check.why: Lake water comes from nature. A tractor is a tool, and a farmer is a person.

check.q: A farm has 300 acres. The farmer plants 100 acres of corn. How many acres are left for soybeans?
check.why: 300 minus 100 is 200 acres.

check.q: Why are natural resources scarce?
choices: There is only so much land and water
They grow back in one day
check.why: Land and water are limited. Using them one way means not using them another way.

lessons.title: Human Resources
lessons.mainIdea: Human resources are the work and skills people bring to making goods and services.
reading: A pizza does not make itself. A cook stretches the dough. A cashier takes the order. The work people do is a *human resource*. Economists also call it labor.
Skills make human resources stronger. A new cook might make 10 pizzas an hour. After practice, the same cook might make 15 an hour (example numbers). That is 5 more pizzas each hour.
People learn skills in school and on the job. Reading, math and teamwork all help. Your learning today is a resource you are building for later. It grows every day.

words.d: the work and skills people use to make goods and services
the work people do to make goods and services

look.title: A Cook Gets Faster
look.cite: Made-up example numbers for this lesson
look.prompt: How many more pizzas an hour does the cook make in Week 4 than in Week 1?

check.q: Which is a human resource?
check.why: Skills and work come from people. Flour is natural; ovens and cars are tools.

check.q: A cook made 10 pizzas an hour, then 15 (example numbers). How many more?
check.why: 15 minus 10 is 5 more pizzas each hour.

check.q: What makes human resources stronger?
check.why: Learning and practice help people do more and better work.

lessons.title: Capital Resources
lessons.mainIdea: Capital resources are tools, machines and buildings made by people to make other things.
reading: The pizza shop has an oven, a mixer and a cutter. These are *capital resources*. People made them. Now they are used to make other things, like pizza.
Good tools help people make more. With a small oven, a shop might bake 4 pizzas at once. With a big oven, it might bake 8 at once (example numbers). That is twice as many.
Money in a jar is not a capital resource. It can buy an oven, but it cannot bake. Capital resources are the real tools. So every shop uses three kinds of resources: natural, human and capital.

words.d: tools, machines and buildings people make and use to make other goods and services
the things used to make goods and services

look.title: Sort the Pizza Shop
look.text: In the pizza shop you see flour, tomatoes, a cook, a cashier, an oven, a mixer and the shop building itself.
look.prompt: Put each thing in a group: natural, human or capital. Which group has the most?

check.q: Which is a capital resource?
check.why: An oven is a tool made by people and used to make pizza.

check.q: A small oven bakes 4 pizzas at once. A big one bakes 8 (example numbers). How many times as many?
check.why: 8 divided by 4 is 2, so the big oven bakes twice as many.

check.q: Is money in a jar a capital resource?
choices: No, it can buy tools but cannot make things itself
No, it is a natural resource
check.why: Capital resources are real tools. Money can buy them but does not do the work.

lessons.title: The Next-Best Thing
lessons.mainIdea: The opportunity cost of a choice is the next-best thing you give up.
reading: The council ranked its ideas. The trip came first. The books came second. So if they pick the trip, they give up the books. The books are the *opportunity cost* of the trip.
Opportunity cost is only the next-best thing. It is not every idea you did not pick. The council did not also give up the balls and movie night as the cost. Only the second choice counts.
Time has an opportunity cost too. Say you spend an hour on video games. If you would have played soccer next, soccer is your opportunity cost. Every *choice* has one.

words.d: the next-best thing you give up when you make a choice
picking one thing from two or more options

look.title: After-School Hour
look.text: Kai has one free hour after school. His top choice is to shoot baskets. His second choice is to read a comic. His third choice is to nap.
look.prompt: If Kai shoots baskets, what is his opportunity cost? Why is the nap not part of it?

check.q: What is opportunity cost?
choices: The next-best thing you give up
check.why: Opportunity cost is only the one next-best choice you gave up.

check.q: Kai shoots baskets. His second choice was reading. His third was a nap. What is his opportunity cost?
check.why: The next-best choice was reading, so that is the cost. It is not a list of everything.

check.q: Does spending time have an opportunity cost?
choices: Yes, you give up the next-best use of that time
check.why: Time is scarce. Using an hour one way means giving up another use of it.

lessons.title: Using a Decision Grid
lessons.mainIdea: A decision grid helps you compare choices by what matters to you.
reading: A *decision grid* is a chart. The choices go across the top. The things that matter go down the side. The things that matter to you are called *criteria*.

The council used three criteria. Does it help many kids? Does it last? Does it fit in $200? Each yes got 1 point. The books got 3 points. The balls got 3 points. Movie night got 2. The trip got 1, because it helps for one day only.
Two ideas tied, so the council voted. The books won. Now the balls were the opportunity cost. The grid did not choose for them. It helped them think clearly.

words.d: a chart that lists choices across the top and what matters down the side
the things that matter to you when you make a choice

look.title: The Council's Grid Scores
look.cite: Scores from the student council story in this chapter
look.prompt: Which two ideas tied? If the council picks the books, what is the opportunity cost?

check.q: In a decision grid, what goes down the side?
check.why: Choices go across the top. The things that matter go down the side.

check.q: An idea gets 1 point for each yes. It gets yes, no, yes. How many points?
check.why: Two yes answers give 1 + 1 = 2 points.

check.q: The council picked the books. The balls were next-best. What was the opportunity cost?
check.why: The opportunity cost is the next-best choice, the balls.

lessons.title: Incentives Change Choices
lessons.mainIdea: Incentives are rewards or costs that make people more or less likely to do something.
reading: A store puts up a sign: juice is $1 today instead of $2 (example prices). More people buy juice. The lower price is an *incentive*. It pulls people toward a choice.
Some incentives are rewards. A library gives a sticker for every 5 books read. Kids read more. Some incentives are costs. A late fee for a library book makes people return it on time.
People compare the reward and the cost. Say a late fee is 10 cents a day (an example). A book 6 days late costs 60 cents. That cost helps people remember to return books.

words.d: a reward or a cost that makes people more or less likely to do something
something good you get for doing something

look.title: The Recycling Deal
look.text: A town pays 5 cents for every can brought back to the store (an example). Before, many cans went in the trash. Now kids collect cans after soccer games.
look.prompt: What is the incentive here? Why did the kids change what they do?

check.q: Which is an incentive?
check.why: A sticker is a reward that makes kids more likely to read.

check.q: A late fee is 10 cents a day (example). A book is 6 days late. What is the fee?
check.why: 6 days times 10 cents is 60 cents.

check.q: Juice drops from $2 to $1 (example prices). What will most shoppers likely do?
check.why: A lower price is an incentive to buy more.

review.why: Scarcity means wants are bigger than what there is, so people must choose.
A tractor is a tool people made to make other goods.

review.q: Maya picks art club. Her second choice was chess. Her third was choir. What is her opportunity cost?
review.why: Only the next-best choice, chess, is the opportunity cost.

review.q: A class has $50. A party costs $35 (example). How much is left?

review.why: Skills and work come from people.

review.q: A shop gives a free cookie with every 10 visits. What is the free cookie?
review.why: It is a reward that makes people more likely to come back.

review.q: In a decision grid, what goes across the top?
review.why: The choices go across the top. What matters goes down the side.

review.q: Which sentence about scarcity is true?
choices: Everyone faces it, even towns and schools
It ends when you save money
review.why: Everyone has limits of time, money or space.

chapters.title: Producers, Consumers and How Work Gets Done
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do people split up work, and what happens when they do?

story.title: The Paper Airplane Race
story.kicker: Two teams fold paper airplanes for ten minutes, and one team tries a new plan.
paragraphs: Ms. Owens held up a stack of paper. "Today we make airplanes," she said. "You have ten minutes. Each plane must fold right and fly past the tape line." Two teams of four sat at two long tables.

The Red Team decided each person would make whole planes alone. Every student folded, creased, drew the wings and tested each plane. Hands moved fast, then slowed down. Kids kept reaching for markers and waiting for a turn at the tape line.

The Blue Team tried something else. Jada folded the first bends. Omar made the wings. Lucy drew the stripes. Ben tested each plane at the line. Each person did one job, over and over. They passed planes down the table like a train.
The timer beeped. Ms. Owens counted. The Red Team had 16 good planes. The Blue Team had 24. "How did you make eight more?" Leo asked. Jada grinned. "We each got really good at one step," she said.
story.think: Why do you think the Blue Team made more planes? Would you rather do one step or every step? Why?

lessons.title: Producers and Consumers
lessons.mainIdea: Producers make goods and services; consumers buy and use them.
reading: A baker makes bread. A bus driver gives rides. People who make goods or give services are *producers*. *Goods* are things you can touch. Services are jobs done for others.
When you buy bread, you are a *consumer*. A consumer buys and uses goods and services. Your family is a consumer at the store. The store is a producer of a service: selling.
Most people are both. A nurse produces care at work. After work, the nurse buys groceries as a consumer. Producers and consumers need each other every day.

words.d: people or businesses that make goods or give services
a person who buys and uses goods and services
things people make that you can touch, like bread or shoes

look.title: A Day at the Mall
look.text: At the mall, a woman cuts hair. A boy buys a pretzel. A man sells shoes. A girl gets her ears checked by a nurse. Later, the hair stylist buys a pretzel too.
look.prompt: Who is a producer? Who is a consumer? Who is both?

check.q: A boy buys a pretzel. What is he?
check.why: He buys and uses the pretzel, so he is a consumer.

check.q: Which is a producer?
check.why: The farmer makes a good, corn, so the farmer is a producer.

check.q: A nurse works all day, then buys food. What is the nurse?
choices: Both a producer and a consumer
check.why: The nurse produces care at work and consumes food after.

lessons.title: Inside a Pizza Shop
lessons.mainIdea: A pizza shop uses natural, human and capital resources to make one pizza.
reading: Look inside a pizza shop. Flour, tomatoes and cheese start on farms. They are made from natural resources. The cook and the cashier are human resources. The oven and the mixer are capital resources.
The shop needs all three kinds. Without flour, there is no dough. Without a cook, nobody makes it. Without an oven, the pizza stays raw. Leave out one kind and there is no pizza.
The shop also pays for each one. Say a pizza sells for $12 (an example). Some pays for flour and cheese. Some pays the cook. Some pays for the oven and rent. What is left is the owner's *profit*.

words.d: the natural, human and capital resources used to make goods and services
the money a business keeps after it pays all its costs

look.title: Where the $12 Goes
look.cite: Made-up example numbers for this lesson
look.prompt: Add the rows. Do they equal $12? Which cost is the smallest?

check.q: In a pizza shop, which is a capital resource?
check.why: The oven is a tool people made to make other goods.

check.q: A pizza sells for $12. Costs are $11 (example). What is the profit?
check.why: $12 minus $11 is $1 profit.

check.q: What happens if the shop has no cook?
check.why: Every kind of resource is needed. Without human resources, nothing gets made.

lessons.title: Starting a Business
lessons.mainIdea: An entrepreneur starts a business, takes a risk and hopes to earn a profit.
reading: Rosa sees kids lose their pencils. She has an idea. She will sell pencil cases at the school fair. Rosa is an *entrepreneur*. An entrepreneur starts a business with a new idea.
Entrepreneurs take a *risk*. Rosa spends $20 on fabric and zippers (an example). She makes 10 cases. If she sells them all for $3 each, she gets $30. Her profit is $30 minus $20, or $10.
But what if only 5 sell? Then she gets $15 and loses $5. That is the risk. Entrepreneurs try anyway, because a good idea can help people and earn a profit.

words.d: a person who starts a business and takes a risk to earn a profit
the chance that you could lose something
the money a business keeps after it pays all its costs

look.title: Rosa's Choice
look.text: Rosa made $10 profit at the fair. Next month there is a bigger fair. She could spend $40 on supplies to make 20 cases. Or she could keep her $10 safe in her piggy bank.
look.prompt: What could Rosa gain? What could she lose? What would you do?

check.q: What does an entrepreneur do?
choices: Starts a business and takes a risk
check.why: An entrepreneur starts a business with an idea and risks losing money.

check.q: Rosa spends $20 and sells 10 cases at $3 each (example). What is her profit?
check.why: 10 times $3 is $30. $30 minus $20 is $10.

check.q: What is the risk for an entrepreneur?
choices: Losing the money spent if sales are low
check.why: If not enough people buy, the business can lose money.

lessons.title: Specialization
lessons.mainIdea: Specialization means doing one kind of job and getting very good at it.
reading: Omar made only wings. After a few minutes, he folded wings very fast. Doing one kind of job is called *specialization*. When you repeat a task, you get quicker and make fewer mistakes.
Grown-ups specialize too. A dentist works on teeth. A pilot flies planes. A baker bakes. Nobody tries to be good at every job. Each person learns one job well.
Specialization also saves time. Omar did not have to switch tools or walk to the tape line. Every minute went to his one step. That time adds up to more planes.

words.d: doing one kind of job and getting very good at it
something a person has learned to do well

look.title: Jobs in a Hospital
look.text: In a hospital, one doctor fixes bones. Another helps babies be born. A cook makes meals. A cleaner keeps rooms safe. A clerk answers phones.
look.prompt: Why doesn't one person do all these jobs? What would happen if they tried?

check.q: What is specialization?
choices: Doing one kind of job well
check.why: Specialization means focusing on one kind of job.

check.q: Why does specialization help people work faster?
choices: They repeat one task and get quicker
check.why: Repeating one task builds skill and saves time switching.

check.q: Which person specializes?
choices: A kid who does every chore once
A dentist who works only on teeth
check.why: The dentist focuses on one kind of job.

lessons.title: The Airplane Assembly Line
lessons.mainIdea: Dividing work into steps, like an assembly line, often makes more goods in the same time.
reading: The Blue Team split one job into four steps. This is called the *division of labor*. A line where work passes from one person to the next is an *assembly line*.
Look at the numbers. In ten minutes, the Red Team made 16 planes. The Blue Team made 24. Both teams had four people. The Blue Team made 8 more planes with the same people and time.
Big factories use assembly lines. In 1913, Henry Ford's company began using a moving assembly line to build cars. Each worker did one step. Cars could be built much faster than before.

words.d: splitting a big job into smaller steps, with different people doing each step
a line where a product moves from worker to worker, and each adds one part

look.title: Planes in Ten Minutes
look.cite: Numbers from the paper airplane story in this chapter
look.prompt: How many more planes did the Blue Team make in ten minutes? Why did both teams start slowly?

check.q: Red made 16 planes. Blue made 24. How many more did Blue make?
check.why: 24 minus 16 is 8.

check.q: What is the division of labor?
choices: Splitting a big job into steps for different people
check.why: The division of labor splits work into steps done by different people.

check.q: Around when did Henry Ford's company start a moving assembly line for cars?
check.why: Ford's moving assembly line began in 1913.

lessons.title: When Splitting Work Is Hard
lessons.mainIdea: The division of labor helps, but jobs can get boring and one slow step can hold up the line.
reading: The assembly line has problems too. Lucy drew stripes for ten minutes straight. By the end, she felt bored. Doing the same small task all day can feel dull.
A line is only as fast as its slowest step. Say Omar folds 3 wings a minute, but Lucy draws only 2 stripes a minute (example numbers). Planes pile up at Lucy. The line makes about 2 planes a minute.
Teams fix this in smart ways. They add a second person to the slow step. They switch jobs so no one gets bored. Good teams look for the slow spot and help it.

words.d: splitting a big job into smaller steps, with different people doing each step
the slowest step in a line of work, which holds up everything after it

look.title: The Sandwich Line
look.text: Four friends make sandwiches for a picnic. One puts bread down, one adds cheese, one adds turkey and one wraps. The wrapper is slow, and sandwiches pile up at the end.
look.prompt: Where is the slow spot? What could the friends change to go faster?

check.q: Omar makes 3 wings a minute. Lucy draws 2 stripes a minute (example). About how many planes a minute can the line finish?
check.why: The line is only as fast as its slowest step, Lucy's 2 a minute.

check.q: What is one problem with doing the same small job all day?
check.why: Repeating one small task can feel dull for workers.

check.q: Sandwiches pile up at the wrapper. What is a smart fix?
check.why: Helping the slowest step lets the whole line go faster.

lessons.title: We Depend on Each Other
lessons.mainIdea: Because people specialize, they depend on each other for most of what they need.
reading: Jada folds planes. But she did not make the paper. She did not make the markers either. Other people did. When people depend on each other like this, it is called *interdependence*.
Think about your breakfast. A farmer grew the wheat. A miller made flour. A baker made bread. A driver brought it to the store. You depend on all of them, and they depend on buyers like you.
Interdependence helps us get more. But if one link breaks, others feel it. A storm can stop trucks. Then stores may run low on bread and milk for a few days.

words.d: when people rely on each other for goods and services
doing one kind of job and getting very good at it

look.title: The Snowy Week
look.text: A big snowstorm closes roads for three days. Trucks cannot reach the grocery store. By Friday, the shelves of milk and bread are almost empty.
look.prompt: Who did the store depend on? Who depends on the store?

check.q: What is interdependence?
choices: Relying on each other for goods and services
check.why: Interdependence means people rely on each other.

check.q: Why does specialization lead to interdependence?
choices: People do one job, so they need others for the rest
check.why: If you do one job, you need others to make the other things you use.

check.q: A storm stops trucks. What likely happens at the store?
choices: The store makes its own milk
check.why: The store depends on trucks. When they stop, goods run low.

lessons.title: A Kid Business
lessons.mainIdea: A small kid business uses resources, specialization and a plan to earn a profit.
reading: Three friends start a car wash. Ava brings buckets and soap. Eli sprays. Mia dries. Each one specializes. Together they are an *entrepreneur* team taking a small risk.
They charge $5 a car (an example price). Soap and sponges cost $10. On Saturday they wash 12 cars. They take in 12 times $5, or $60. Their profit is $60 minus $10, or $50.
They split the $50 three ways. Each gets about $16, with $2 left over for next week's soap. They keep a notebook of costs and sales. That helps them plan their next *business* day.

words.d: a group that makes or sells goods or services to earn money
a person who starts a business and takes a risk to earn a profit

look.title: Car Wash Saturday
look.cite: Made-up example numbers for this lesson
look.prompt: If they washed 14 cars instead, how much money would they take in?

check.q: They wash 12 cars at $5 each (example). How much money comes in?
check.why: 12 times $5 is $60.

check.q: They take in $60 and spend $10. What is the profit?
check.why: $60 minus $10 is $50.

check.q: Eli only sprays and Mia only dries. What is this?
check.why: Each friend does one job, which is specialization.

lessons.title: Making More With Less
lessons.mainIdea: Better tools, skills and teamwork help people make more in the same amount of time.
reading: The car wash team gets a hose with a spray nozzle. Before, they washed 2 cars an hour. Now they wash 3 an hour (example numbers). Making more in the same time is called *productivity*.
Three things raise productivity. Better tools, like the hose, are capital resources. More skill comes from practice. Teamwork comes from dividing the work well.
Higher productivity helps everyone. Workers can earn more for each hour. Buyers can get more goods. That is why businesses and schools care about learning and good tools.

words.d: how much is made in a certain amount of time
tools, machines and buildings people make and use to make other goods and services

look.title: The New Hose
look.text: The team washed 2 cars an hour with buckets. With the new hose, they wash 3 cars an hour. The hose cost $15 (example price). They work 4 hours each Saturday.
look.prompt: How many more cars can they wash each Saturday now? Was the hose a good choice?

check.q: What is productivity?
choices: How much is made in a set amount of time
check.why: Productivity measures output in a certain amount of time.

check.q: They wash 2 cars an hour, then 3 (example). How many more in 4 hours?
check.why: Before: 4 times 2 is 8. After: 4 times 3 is 12. 12 minus 8 is 4.

check.q: Which one raises productivity?
check.why: More skill helps people make more in the same time.

review.why: A consumer buys and uses goods and services.

review.q: What is the division of labor?
choices: Splitting a job into steps for different people
review.why: It splits a big job into steps done by different people.

review.q: An entrepreneur spends $30 and takes in $45 (example). What is the profit?
Why do specialized workers depend on each other?
choices: Each makes only part of what people need
review.why: Doing one job means you need others for the rest.

review.q: A line has steps that take 4, 5 and 2 units a minute. What limits the line?
review.why: A line goes only as fast as its slowest step.

review.q: Which is a human resource in a bakery?
review.why: Work and skill come from people.

review.q: A worker makes 5 toys an hour, then 7 with a new tool (example). What went up?
review.why: Making more in the same time is higher productivity.

review.q: What risk does an entrepreneur take?
choices: Losing money if not enough people buy
review.why: An entrepreneur spends money first and may not earn it back.
